analysis:
Retrieval is the main problem. not_retrieved accounts for 82 of the 84 failures. recall_at_k is 0.43, while verifier_recall is 0.98 and fp_earlier is only 0.02. So the verifier handles almost every true quote it is shown, but most true quotes never reach it.

The failing statements are heavy paraphrases. They swap in synonyms ("not voiced any objections" for "haven't raised any issues") and replace the speaker's name with a role ("an official", "a pop singer", "a Vancouver team official"). That leaves BM25 with few overlapping words, so the true quote often ranks below position 30.

It also means the speaker-related retrieval settings add little and may add noise. Usually there is no name in the statement to match, and role words like "official", "said", "prime minister" or "team" pull in unrelated quotes.

The cheapest broad fix is a deeper candidate pool. Batches can be made larger at the same time so verifier calls per claim stay at 2. The other two levers are taking the role and reporting wording out of the query, and searching quote text only. The single rejected_by_verifier case and the single 13-minute timing miss are too rare to target.

rationale: Targets not_retrieved. With anonymised statements, indexing speaker names rarely helps the true quote. Instead it lets quotes whose speaker field happens to match a common query word outrank the true quote. Searching the quote text alone ('quotation' index) should improve ranking on content. Verifier calls stay the same.

Targets not_retrieved (82 of 84 failures). The true quotes are paraphrases with little word overlap, so they often rank just outside the top 30. Doubling k to 60 should recover a good share of them. Raising batch from 15 to 30 at the same time keeps calls_per_claim at 2. Verifier recall is 0.98, which leaves room for a small drop from bigger batches. The prompt's strict completeness and extent rules should keep extra earlier false positives in check.

Targets not_retrieved. Statements usually name the speaker only by role or description ("an official said", "a Democratic challenger argued"). In the content_plus_speaker template those words become query terms and match many unrelated quotes that share them. The 'content' template drops the 'X said that' framing, so BM25 weights the claim's actual content words. Verifier calls stay the same.

analysis:
I'm targeting not_retrieved, which is 82 of the 84 failures. The verifier is not the problem: verifier recall is 0.98 and only 2% of claims got a wrong, earlier match. The problem is that BM25 puts the true quotation in the top 30 for only 43% of claims.

The failing statements are heavy paraphrases. The speaker is usually replaced by a role ("an official", "a pop singer"), and most content words are swapped for synonyms. Simple query-side changes have already been tried and failed:
- Switching the index to quote text only changed nothing.
- Dropping the speaker from the query cost 4 claims.
- Doubling k to 60 (batch 30) gained only 1 claim net, below the threshold of 3. My guess is that the extra 30 candidates brought in about as many plausible wrong-speaker quotes, some of them earlier, as true quotes they recovered. I haven't checked this against the logs.

So the most promising route is to keep the larger candidate pool but make it cleaner: use the untried speaker filter to drop quotes from other named speakers (unattributed quotes are kept), or warn the verifier about speaker mismatches. Both should keep the extra recall while removing what likely cancelled it last time, and the filter also cuts verifier calls.

One open risk: I don't know whether the surname filter is applied before or after the top-k cut. If it is applied after, it can't raise recall, only precision and cost. Also, when the statement names no person there is no surname to filter on, so the filter may do nothing for those claims.

rationale: Widen the pool to k=60 to recover true quotes ranked 31-60, and turn on the surname speaker filter to remove quotes from clearly different named speakers (unattributed quotes stay). This is materially different from the rejected k=60/batch=30 change: that one probably gained true quotes but also added wrong-speaker distractors and earlier false matches, and the filter targets exactly those. Batch stays at 15. Because the filter shrinks the list, verifier calls should stay near the current 2 per claim instead of doubling.

Cheap screen: turn on the surname speaker filter alone at k=30. If the filter is applied before the top-k cut, it frees slots for lower-ranked true quotes from the right speaker and raises recall@k for free. Either way it reduces verifier calls and earlier false matches. Its result also shows how the filter interacts with retrieval, which decides whether the first proposal is worth it.

Same idea, but handled by the verifier instead of a hard filter: k=60 with speaker_hint on, so each candidate is marked as matching, mismatching or unknown speaker. This keeps any true quote whose speaker was attributed wrongly, which a hard filter would drop, while helping the verifier reject the extra different-speaker distractors that likely cancelled the earlier k=60 gain. Cost: about 4 calls per claim at batch 15.

analysis: Almost every failure is not_retrieved (82 of 84). Verifier recall is 0.98 and earlier-article false positives are 2%, so the ceiling is BM25 recall@k at 0.43. The failing statements are heavy paraphrases that often hide the speaker ("an official said", "a pop singer"), so they share few words with the original quote. That also explains past results: speaker-based retrieval hurt or did nothing (speaker filter cut recall@k to about 0.20; the quote-only index changed nothing), and stripping the reporting frame from the query cost 4 net claims. Doubling k to 60 gained only one claim, so the true quote is often far down the ranking or not lexically reachable at all. The knobs can only make small gains here. Raw-query retrieval has never been tried and costs nothing to screen, so I rank it first. Second is a moderate k increase that keeps verifier calls at 2 per claim. Third is a query/index pairing that hasn't been tried as a pair.
